settings.heading: Who We Are
settings.text: ARTSofINDIA.in - Traditional Arts and Crafts from India, is an initiative from 'Sanskriti', which is registered in Bangalore, India. The portal represents the inter-cultural moments of India, when new perspectives arise and much that has been forgotten is rediscovered and replayed. The goal of Sanskriti is to help Indian Traditional Arts and artists get the recognition on global art map.

settings.heading: What We Do
settings.intro: For the past one decade, we have been promoting Indian arts and crafts and providing a much-needed platform for the mostly poor and remotely situated artists on these arts.

settings.heading: Our Social Responsibility
settings.intro: We are part of our society and we truly understand the responsibilities we have towards it. Not all artists are poor, but most are, and these artists play a crucial role in keeping Indian traditional arts alive. They need proper care, or we might lose the arts along with them. We support them in these ways:
settings.closing: We hope to revive the forgotten and slowly vanishing traditional arts of India and their artists with our sincere efforts.

settings.text: Listing their art works on ArtsOfIndia with sufficient details at minimum cost
Helping them find buyers and close the deal
Helping them participate in art events, workshops and exhibitions
Connecting them with people interested in learning the arts

settings.heading: Artisans in India
settings.body:
The artisan sector has enormous untapped potential to drive economic and community development and preserve cultural heritage in the developing world. Artisans play a major role in developing communities and local economies. Second only to agriculture, artisan enterprise is the second largest employer in the developing world. In India alone, seven million artisans make a living using traditional skills and techniques to create handmade products. Artisan crafts are proven sources of job creation, export earnings, poverty alleviation, promotion of cultural diversity, and skills building and human capital investment.

From early ages, the people of India have used handmade products. In ancient India people lived in tribal colonies and made utility items for daily need. Then they started selling these products in local markets called 'Haat'. As demand grew, those who made handicrafts began trading their work more widely.

Skilled people create everything from consumer goods to decorative pieces out of paper, wood, clay, shells, rock, stone and metal, using simple tools. India is known for its ethnicity, and the artisan sector is the gateway to this ethnic nation. India is among the most culturally rich countries in the world, and its skilled artisans have spread the fame of Indian handicrafts around the globe. Many rural people still earn their livelihood from their creative work.

Examples of Indian art and craft can be seen in forts, palaces, architecture and miniature paintings. Miniature paintings are colourful, handmade and small, known for intricate and delicate brushwork. The colours are handmade from minerals, vegetables, precious stones, indigo, conch shells, pure gold and silver. Every state has its own painting technique. States known for their arts, culture and paintings include Bihar, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Assam and Himachal Pradesh.

settings.name: Kislay Komal
settings.text: An engineer by education, IT professional by profession and Indian at heart, rooted in his homeland Bihar. Over a decade he has worked with artists to promote Indian traditional arts. He started mithilapaintings.com in 2006, co-founded 'Sanskriti' in 2010 as a collaboration platform for arts and artists, and launched the ecommerce venture ArtsofIndia.in in 2016.

settings.name: Jyoti Sharma
settings.text: An MBA by education, she worked in the corporate world before moving to the US. A homemaker with two kids, she always wanted to stay connected with India and its arts and culture. She joined Kislay to take Sanskriti forward and help hundreds of artists reach beyond India's boundaries.

settings.name: Mamta Bharti
settings.text: A Madhubani artist from Bihar, associated with Sanskriti since its inception and now leading operations in the Bihar region. A State Award winner, she completed Intermediate Arts from Bihar Intermediate Council, a B.F.A. (Applied) from the Arts & Crafts College of Patna University, and an EDP in fashion designing from SISI, Patna. She learnt Madhubani, Tikuli, Tantra Kala, Manjusha, Godna and other folk arts at Upendra Maharathi Shilp Anusandhan Sansthan. Born with a disability, she is a living example of courage, determination and women's empowerment.

settings.name: Shweta
settings.text: A known Madhubani artist who has shown her collections in exhibitions across the globe. A folk artist since 1997, she has trained more than five hundred rural and urban students. Awards include 1st in the International Poster Contest 1996 and 2nd in 1997 (NCERT and UNFPA), an award from the Government of Delhi in 1997, and a Global Runner-up award from the USA in 1996 for the theme 'Where we live now'. She was also part of the world's longest painting (325 m) in 1999.

settings.name: Saurabh Atirek
settings.text: A doctor by profession, settled in Russia, and enthusiastic about Indian tradition, arts and crafts. He left India in 1998 to pursue his career but never forgot his roots, and spreads awareness of India's arts and crafts wherever he goes. Fluent in Russian, he is creating a market for Sanskriti products there.

settings.name: Kalyan Joshi
settings.text: Famous Phad artist who began working with his father and guru, Padma Shri awardee Shri Shrilal Joshi, at age eight. He experimented with Phad painting using new stories and contemporary styles (collage and line drawing), created picture montages, and experimented with character animation. Founder of 'ANKAN' Kala Sansthan, which has taught Phad painting to thousands of children. In 15 years he organized 30 exhibitions in Bhilwara.

settings.name: Manoj Kumar Pandit
settings.text: Famously known as Manjusha Guru, one of the biggest artists of Manjusha Art. He is known for reviving Manjusha and saving it from vanishing. He trains many budding Manjusha artists at his training center in Bhagalpur, Bihar, and has received the Bihar State Award and several other awards.

settings.name: Venkat Raman Singh Shyam
settings.text: A noted Gond and contemporary Indian artist who works with murals, etchings, mixed media and animation. He has travelled extensively and exhibited in India and abroad. Awarded the Rajya Hasta Shilpa Puraskar by the Government of Madhya Pradesh in 2002. He coordinated an animated film on a Gond folktale by Tara Douglas that won the Tallest Story Competition Trophy at the Inverness Film Festival, Scotland, in 2007.

settings.name: Vinay Sharma
settings.text: A noted contemporary artist with a Diploma in Painting and a Post Graduation from the University of Baroda (1990). Solo shows include the Gallery of Contemporary Art in Poland, Hanover Galleries Liverpool, Talisin Arts Centre at Swansea University and Hope Street Art Gallery, Liverpool. Group shows in India and abroad include Germany, UK, Australia, Korea, Jaipur, New Delhi and Mumbai. Honors include an Honorable Mention from National Lalit Kala Akademi, the Golden Jubilee of India's Independence Award (Rajasthan) from AIFACS, the All Rajasthan Drawing Award, an All India Award for Print, and Rajasthan State Awards.

settings.intro: Our goal is to improve the lives and livelihoods of India's skilled rural handicraft and handloom artisans, who produce objects of great beauty with strong market potential by practicing the rich and varied Indian handicraft tradition.
